sentences.text: Abrictosaurus was a bipedal herbivore or omnivore and represents one of the most basal members of the heterodontosaurid family.
The animal measured approximately 1.2 meters in length and weighed less than 45 kilograms.

This creature is best known for possessing large, canine-like tusks in both the upper and lower jaws, while the front of the jaws lacked teeth and instead featured a hard beak used for cropping vegetation.
The upper caniniform tooth measured 10.5 millimeters high, while the lower counterpart reached 17 millimeters.
Large, canine-like tusks appeared in both the upper and lower jaws of this small dinosaur.
It possessed smaller, less powerful forelimbs with one fewer phalanx bone in the fourth and fifth digits compared to Heterodontosaurus.
Richard Thulborn first described the holotype specimen in 1974, initially naming it Lycorhinus consors.
The name Abrictosaurus, meaning 'wakeful lizard', reflects Hopson's disagreement with Thulborn's hypothesis that heterodontosaurids aestivated.
Researchers suggested that the lack of tusks in one specimen indicated it was female, or possibly a female of a different species.
It is debated whether the lack of tusks represents sexual dimorphism or is instead a juvenile trait, as the specimen may be a juvenile.
The animal is classified within the family Heterodontosauridae.
Abrictosaurus belongs to the subfamily Heterodontosaurinae.
It is a member of the ornithischian dinosaur clade.
The presence of caniniforms in the second specimen supports the classification of Abrictosaurus consors as a valid species.
The fossils date to the Hettangian and Sinemurian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 200 to 190 million years ago.
The time range for Abrictosaurus is estimated from 201.4 to 192.9 million years ago.
The habitat consisted of sand dunes and seasonal floodplains within a semiarid environment with sporadic rainfall.
Thulborn continued to classify Lycorhinus angustidens, Heterodontosaurus tucki, and Abrictosaurus consors as species within the genus Lycorhinus.
